newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban's Afghan rule looks shaky after two weeks.
newsitem.headline: Taleban's Afghan rule looks shaky after two weeks.

text.p: The Taleban's two-week old administration looked precarious on Friday as its militia faced guerrilla assaults near the Afghan capital and the prospect of military alliance among its foes in the north.

Local commanders and units loyal to former military chief Ahmad Rashid Masood attacked the Taleban behind its frontline, including its Bagram airbase 30 miles (50 km) north of Kabul, travellers and Reuters photographer Patrick de Noirmont said.

The Taleban, whose purist brand of Islam has brought security to territory under its control but has raised alarm over its restrictions on women, said it was ready for talks with Masood and militia commander Abdul Rashid Dostum.
"We call on both of them for talks," said Maulvi Wakil Ahmad, a member of the Taleban supreme council, or shura, contacted in the Pakistani city of Quetta.
"They must not select the path of fighting because this is a bloody path. If they impose fighting on the government, the government will strongly defend itself."
Uzbek chief Dostum, Masood and Karim Khalilli, head of the Shia Hezb-i-Wahadat, pledged in a meeting in the Dostum-held north to unite against the Taleban unless fighting stopped.
The leaders also called for a meeting of all faction leaders to form a "permanent government of Afghanistan" and agreed to set up a Supreme Defence Council whose composition was to be decided later.

In Kabul, the Taleban's acting deputy foreign minister, Sher Mohammad Stanakzai, said it supported U.N. moves for a ceasefire and had agreed to efforts by special envoy Norbert Holl to arrange talks between the Taleban and other groups.

Fighting has erupted on the plains between Taleban-held Kabul and the Hindu Kush -- mountains forming a natural defence for both Masood, who holds his native Panjsher valley, and Dostum, who controls six provinces north of the Salang tunnel.

Bypassing the Taleban's frontline, Masood has persuaded local commanders in villages on the plain to launch guerrilla attacks on the Taleban's lines of communication with the capital, travellers said on Friday.

Fleeing villagers said men from Saray Khoeja, near the airbase, had turned on the Taleban militia. The sound of automatic rifles and rocket-propelled grenades filled the air as civilians fled the village.
The airbase itself later came under shellfire from former government forces, witnesses said. Shelling lasted for about an hour and Taleban militia responded with helicopter gunships.
At least six shells landed inside the perimeter in the first apparent attack on the base since the Taleban overran the capital and the plains north of it late last month.

The Taleban have admitted only minor losses and limited casualties since Masood's forces launched their counter-attack earlier this week. Its officials have blamed Western media for exaggerating gains made by Masood.
The Taleban have previously said they have no quarrel with Dostum, a former communist army chief, but have demanded Masood surrender.

But its offensive against Masood's Panjsher stronghold, launched a week ago, quickly stalled after Taleban fighters made little headway beyond two peaks, progressing only a few hundred metres (yards) down the 150 km (100 mile) valley.
Masood successfully defended the valley against Soviet forces in the 1980s, earning himself the nickname "Lion of the Panjsher".
In the past he has been both enemy and ally to Dostum, whose well-equipped fighting force has long protected a six-province domain in the north.

Afghan watchers said that while moderate elements in the Taleban, born barely two years ago near the Pakistani border, may welcome talks with the two, more purist Taleban leaders may want to push through their Jihad (Holy War) to its conclusion.
